hook.text: A hospital buys a model that predicts which patients will deteriorate. In testing, it works beautifully.

live.text: Then it goes live on the wards, and the alerts start coming in.

who.text: But nobody decided who should respond. Should the nurse check the patient? Should a doctor order a test? Should someone call the intensive care team?

bounce.text: So the alert bounces around. Everyone sees it. No one owns it.

result.text: The result: more work for the staff, and no better outcomes for the patients. Knowing that a problem may happen is useful only if you can do something about it.

six.text: Prediction is only the beginning. Here are six steps from prediction to action.

s1.text: One. Define the target exactly. Deterioration within six hours? Twenty-four hours? Seven days?

s2.text: Two. Use only the information that exists at the moment of prediction. Peeking at data from the future is called leakage, and it makes results look unrealistically good.

s3.text: Three. Estimate the risk with a validated model. A model that worked in another hospital still needs testing in yours.

s4.text: Four. Choose a threshold. That decides who gets an alert.

s5.text: Five. Link the alert to a response. Who does what, and how fast? For example: the nurse reviews the patient within thirty minutes.

s6.text: Six. Measure the whole process. Did patient outcomes improve? Did unnecessary tests go up?

end.text: A good prediction with no response plan is just noise. The value comes from the decision it improves.
